General American is the prestige accent of the United States, standardized in network television and radio broadcasting in the mid-twentieth century. Rhotic, with relatively uniform vowel values and minimal regional coloring, it lacks the strong local identity markers of regional accents and remains the reference standard for American English in formal and educational contexts.

The most defining feature is rhotic pronunciation, where the r is pronounced in all positions, including after vowels in words like "car" and "here" and word-finally in "butter." Another significant feature is the cot-caught merger, where "cot" and "caught" are pronounced identically, a feature absent from RP and conservative American accents.

Flapping is another characteristic, where the t and d sounds become a single tap in unstressed syllables, so "butter" and "udder" sound nearly identical. Tense-lax vowel distinctions are relatively symmetrical and clear compared to British English vowel systems. The r is typically pronounced as a retroflex approximant, with the tongue curled back and less prominent than in rhotic British accents.

General American emerged as a broadcast standard partly due to its perceived neutrality and lack of strong regional or class associations. It stands as one of the two main reference accents for global English, alongside Received Pronunciation, the British prestige standard. Southern American English shows systematic vowel shifts and grammatical structures distinct from General American, while Upper Midwestern American English, a regional variant, approaches General American closely and was historically preferred in broadcasting.
